items.title: Tasmota SwitchMode 11/12 Example - v1.1
items.text: Updated August, 2020. Changelog at last page

items.title: Tasmota SwitchMode 11/12 wall switch implementation with Home Assistant / ControllerX
items.text:
Want to make your 'dumb' wall switches smart and at the same time improve installation of smart lights WAF 👩‍🦰 ? Then the solution could be to 'Tasmotize' your wall switches, and use Home Assistant with the ControllerX app to control the smart light connected to that switch. With this setup, you'll be able to toggle, turn lights on at full brightness, sync and dim your lights directly from your wall switch. Today, many WIFI switches are so small, that they can fit behind wall outlets/switches or in ceiling outlets. Personally, I've used Shelly One devices and Itead Sonoff Mini's. Both are easy to flash with Tasmota using either USB-to-UART adapter or directly OTA. No soldering is actually needed these days. The flash part and build instructions are too comprehensive to elaborate on further in this documentation. Instructions are 'out there' - Google it! 😉

One of my Sonoff Mini installations behind a wall switch. Danish wall switch modules are typically not larger than appx. 50x50mm pr. module (outside measurements). I’ve LK Opus 66 installed, which is a slightly larger type measuring 66mm in width. Still I can squeeze a Sonoff Mini in behind a ‘typical’ double module wall switch. Shelly devices are a bit smaller, round in shape and in general easier to fit than the Sonoff Mini’s.

One final warning: Using Shelly/Sonoff devices behind wall switches/outlets involves fiddling with ⚡HIGH VOLTAGE⚡ that could potentially INJURE OR KILL YOU 🩸😱💀, if not handled/installed correctly !! Furthermore, local building code might prohibit use of such devices in wall outlets and unauthorized installation will most likely be illegal in most countries. If you don't know EXACTLY what you're doing - then DON'T proceed with this project !! Now you've been warned !!

Following example is with a Shelly One device, placed in the wall socket behind the switch, to control an Ikea WS bulb in the ceiling outlet. The bulb is connected to Home Assistant via Zigbee2MQTT. I've refitted my wall switch with a spring, so it'll act like a push button.

The Switchmode11/12 option in Tasmota, gives the user six different switch commands to be used for automation. With ControllerX only four of these commands are needed, as ControllerX internally controls changes in dimming direction. These commands (events) are sent directly to ControllerX via MQTT.

items.title: Switchmode11/12 Tasmota output commands are:
items.text:
Switchstate=2: toggle (Normal TOGGLE function. One single press)
Switchstate=4: inc-dec (HOLD function. Sent after delay defined with Setoption32)
Switchstate=5: inv (INVERSE dim direction function. Not used in this implementation, as ControllerX handles this internally)
Switchstate=6: clear (Delayed RELEASE function. Sent when button is released AFTER delay defined with Setoption32. Not used in this implementation)
Switchstate=7: clear (Normal RELEASE function. Sent immediately after button is released)
Switchstate=8: double (DOUBLE press function. Two consecutive presses within time delay defined with SetOption32)

items.title: Requirements:
items.text:
Tasmota: v8.4.0.2 or newer

ControllerX: v3.4.0b1 or newer

items.title: Shelly device Tasmota setup (Use switchmode 11 !!):
items.text: Module type: Shelly 1 (46):

items.title: Sonoff Mini device Tasmota setup (Use switchmode 12 !!):
items.text:
Module type: Sonoff Basic (1)

GPIO4: Switch1 (9)

items.title: Setup ControllerX app:
items.text:
Both examples listed below will:

  • toggle light(s) upon single button press
  • dim light(s) up/down when button is held
  • Turn light(s) on at full brightness upon double press

First example is with two separate controllers. This will also handle HOLD FROM LIGHTS OFF situation. Which, when lights are off, will SYNC light/lights when button is held for 0,8 sec.

items.title: ControllerX apps.yaml example no. 1:
items.text:
controller_switchmode11_on:
  module: controllerx
  class: LightController
  controller: tasmota_topic # Normally z2m friendly name. Here topic used in Tasmota rules
  integration: state
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
    action_key: action  # Defaults to action if not specified
  light: light.your_light # define your own light entity
  constrain_input_boolean: light.your_light,on # This whole configuration will work when the light is on
  mapping:
    toggle: toggle
    inc-dec: hold_brightness_toggle
    clear: release
    double: on_full_brightness

controller_switchmode11_off:
  module: controllerx
  class: LightController
  controller: tasmota_topic # Normally z2m friendly name. Here topic used in Tasmota rules
  integration: state
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
    action_key: action  # Defaults to action if not specified
  light: light.your_light # define your own light entity
  constrain_input_boolean: light.your_light,off # This whole configuration will work when the light is off
  mapping:
    toggle: toggle
    inc-dec: sync
    double: on_full_brightness

Second example is a more simple setup, where smooth_power_on is enabled instead, when button is held from lights off position.

items.title: ControllerX apps.yaml example no. 2:
items.text:
tasmota_switchmode11:
  module: controllerx
  class: LightController
  controller: tasmota_topic  # Normally z2m friendly name. Here topic used in Tasmota rules
  integration: state
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
    action_key: action  # Defaults to action if not specified
  smooth_power_on: true # enable 'smooth power on' feature when button is held from lights off
  delay: 250 # change delay if you want faster/slower dimming response (default: 350 ms.)
  light: light.your_light # define your own light entity
  mapping:
    toggle: toggle
    inc-dec: hold_brightness_toggle
    clear: release
    double: on_full_brightness

items.title: Notes on Appdaemon and HA's state machine:
items.text:
Things unfortunately take time when HA's state machine is involved! This can be noticeable for some (for others not), when AppDaemon apps have to check HA states, e.g. by using constrain_input_boolean (as in example 1) or change HA states by toggling lights. In my setup, using a constrain_input_boolean adds some 100 ms. delay on execution. Not much on its own, but still worth to keep in mind. Toggling lights via HA automation is also some 100 ms. faster than toggling through Appdaemon/ControllerX. So in order to get the fastest possible toggle of lights, I'm personally using a simple HA automation for toggling lights and let ControllerX handle everything else 🙂

Optional HA toggle automation below. Remember to remove toggle from mapping in Appdaemon/ControllerX apps.yaml 😉

# Toggle lights through HA using direct MQTT events. Quicker response than using platform state or directly in appdaemon ControllerX app
- alias: tasmota_switchmode11_toggle
  trigger:
    platform: mqtt
    topic: zigbee2mqtt/tasmota_topic
    payload: "{\"action\": \"toggle\"}" # escape characters needed !
  action:
    service: light.toggle
    data:
      entity_id:
      light.your_light

items.title: Setup needed commands and rules in Tasmota software via console:
items.text:
Powerretain1 1    Retain Tasmota power settings in HA in event of power outage
Setoption1 1      Allow only single, double and hold press button actions
Setoption32 8     Delay for HOLD button (in 0,1 sec.). I use 8 = 0,8 sec. Max value allowed is 63 !!
Setoption34 50    Minimize delay between backlog commands to 50 ms. (Default 200 ms.)
Switchtopic 0     Disable switchtopic. Needed when using rules in Tasmota.
Switchmode1 11    Set Tasmota to switchmode11


RULE1
on switch1#state=2 do publish zigbee2mqtt/tasmota_topic {"action": "toggle"} endon
on switch1#state=8 do publish zigbee2mqtt/tasmota_topic {"action": "double"} endon
on switch1#state=7 do backlog publish zigbee2mqtt/tasmota_topic {"action": "clear"};rule3 1 endon

RULE2
on mqtt#disconnected do rule1 0 endon
on mqtt#connected do rule1 1 endon

RULE3 5
on switch1#state=4 do backlog publish zigbee2mqtt/tasmota_topic {"action": "inc-dec"};rule3 0 endon

NB: Note the extra decimal '5' in RULE3 !!

RULE1 sends the TOGGLE and DOUBLE press command via MQTT . CLEAR command is fired upon button release and RULE3 is enabled again (ready for next HOLD command).

RULE2 handles the 'fall back' to direct switch control if MQTT server is unavailable. Nice WAF feature, if HA/MQTT server is down. Then lights still can be toggled on/off using the wall switch.

RULE3 sends the HOLD command and disables itself (to ensure only one HOLD command is fired).

RULE3 is set as 'run once' in Tasmota (with the decimal 5 after the rule number) to prevent extra HOLD commands from being fired before the rule is disabled.

Rules also need to be 'escaped', if used with HA automation. Tasmota will automatically add needed escape characters, if rules are entered without.

items.text:
doc v1.0:

  • Initial example documentation May, 2020

  • Deprecated use of custom controllers in example. These will shortly be deprecated as well in ControllerX

items.title: Enable MQTT Plugin
items.text: If we want to use the mqtt or tasmota integrations, listen_to: mqtt in the z2m integration, or the Z2MLightController with mode: mqtt, we need to enable the AppDaemon MQTT plugin. How to do it depends on how you installed ControllerX.

items.title: ControllerX app
items.text:
1. Go to Settings → Apps → ControllerX → Configuration.
  2. Turn on Enable MQTT.
  3. If you use the Mosquitto broker app, that's all: the app gets the broker address and credentials from Home Assistant. Otherwise, fill in MQTT host (without the port, e.g. 192.168.1.10), MQTT port, MQTT username and MQTT password. They are under Show unused optional configuration options.
  4. Save. Home Assistant offers to restart the app.

The app manages the AppDaemon configuration itself, so there's no appdaemon.yaml to edit. It connects to the broker with a client ID generated for each install, so several ControllerX apps (for example, in two Home Assistant instances) can share the same broker. To use a client ID of your own, set MQTT client ID.

items.title: AppDaemon app
items.text:
Add the following highlighted section to the AppDaemon configuration (/app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/appdaemon.yaml):

---
appdaemon:
  latitude: X.XXXXXXX
  longitude: X.XXXXXXX
  elevation: XXXX
  time_zone: XXXXXXXX
  missing_app_warnings: 0 # (1)
  plugins:
    HASS:
      type: hass
      token: !env_var SUPERVISOR_TOKEN
    MQTT:
      type: mqtt
      namespace: mqtt # This is important
      client_id: appdaemon # (2)
      client_host: core-mosquitto # (3)
      client_user: XXXXX # (4)
      client_password: !secret mqtt_password # (5)
      client_topics: NONE # (6)
http:
  url: http://0.0.0.0:5050
admin:
api:
  1. Extra tip: you can add missing_app_warnings if you don't want any warning spam from ControllerX when starting AppDaemon.
  2. A name no other MQTT client uses. Without it, AppDaemon connects as appdaemon_mqtt_client, so if two AppDaemon instances use the same broker, the broker keeps disconnecting one of them.
  3. core-mosquitto if you use the Mosquitto broker app. Otherwise, the host of your MQTT broker without the port (e.g. 192.168.1.10).
  4. The user and password of your MQTT broker.
  5. Add mqtt_password: <your password> to secrets.yaml, next to appdaemon.yaml (or to the file set in secrets:, if your appdaemon.yaml has that line). You can also write the password here directly.
  6. Optional. By default, AppDaemon subscribes to every MQTT topic (#) and receives every message in the broker, even though ControllerX only needs the topics of your controllers. With NONE, ControllerX subscribes to just those topics. Leave it out if other AppDaemon apps of yours listen to MQTT topics without subscribing to them.

Then restart the AppDaemon app.

items.title: What's AppDaemon and why I need it
items.text:
AppDaemon lets you write Home Assistant automations in Python instead of YAML. For simple automations, YAML or the automation editor are great, but when automations get more complicated, they become difficult to manage in YAML. This is where AppDaemon comes in.

This is the reason this project is built on top of AppDaemon. Now you might be convinced, but have no idea how to install and set it up. If you are using Home Assistant OS, the installation page explains your options: the ControllerX app, which includes its own AppDaemon, or the AppDaemon app from the app store with ControllerX installed in it, either through AppDaemon Store or manually.
path: What's AppDaemon and why I need it

items.title: Update ControllerX
items.text:
How to update ControllerX depends on how you installed it:

  • ControllerX app: update the app from Settings → Apps. The app restarts on its own.
  • AppDaemon Store: update ControllerX from the AppDaemon Store UI (or enable auto-update). AppDaemon Store restarts the AppDaemon app on its own (see AppDaemon Store and AppDaemon app).
  • Manual installation: replace the controllerx folder with the latest release and restart the AppDaemon app (see Manual installation).

With a manual installation, remember to restart AppDaemon after installing a new version of ControllerX, since AppDaemon does not reimport the modules. If AppDaemon is not restarted, it will keep running the old version.

items.title: Zigbee2MQTT - HA sensor is deprecated
items.text:
Zigbee2MQTT HA sensor deprecated since ControllerX v4.29.0

Zigbee2MQTT 2.0.0 brought some breaking changes, and one of them was to deprecate the Home Assistant action sensors, which is the default option of the Zigbee2MQTT integration in ControllerX.

You might be here because of a warning in the AppDaemon logs that looks like the following:

Quote

⚠️ Listening to HA sensor actions is now deprecated and will be removed in the future. Use listen_to: mqtt or listen_to: event instead. Read more about it here: https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/others/z2m-ha-sensor-deprecated

This might be because your controller configuration looks like:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller
  controller: sensor.livingroom_controller_action
  integration: z2m
  light: light.livingroom

The issue is integration: z2m, which reads a HA sensor by default. You need to switch to either mqtt (recommended) or HA event (experimental).

items.title: Switch to MQTT listener (recommended)
items.text:
To switch to MQTT (as recommended by Zigbee2MQTT), you first need to enable the MQTT plugin. Then, change your configuration to something like the following:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller
  controller: livingroom_controller # (1)
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt # (2)
  light: light.livingroom
  1. This is the friendly name of the device in Zigbee2MQTT. Check here how to get this value.
  2. With mqtt, ControllerX listens to the MQTT topic of the controller.

items.title: Switch to HA Event sensor listener (experimental)
items.text:
Another option is to listen to the new (and experimental) event entity from Zigbee2MQTT 2.0.0. First, enable the experimental feature in Zigbee2MQTT as explained here. Then, change your configuration to something like:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller
  controller: livingroom_controller_action # (1)
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: event # (2)
  light: light.livingroom
  1. This is the event entity without the event. prefix. Check here how to get this value.
  2. With event, ControllerX listens to the changes of the event entity.

items.title: Zigbee2MQTT Light Controller
items.text:
This is supported since ControllerX v4.21.0

ControllerX has always supported the Light Controller, which, amongst other features, smoothly changes attributes (brightness, color temperature) by periodically requesting the changes to Home Assistant. This works with lights from many integrations (e.g. Zigbee2MQTT, deCONZ, WLED, Hue). However, this generalization penalizes Zigbee2MQTT, which has its own mechanism to change the brightness and color temperature over time, and works much more smoothly than the Light Controller.

Zigbee2MQTT allows sending a payload like {"brightness_move": -40} to the zigbee2mqtt/FRIENDLY_NAME/set topic, which decreases the brightness 40 steps per second over time. Then, we can send the following payload to the same topic to make it stop: {"brightness_move": "stop"}. Zigbee2MQTT does not have a specific page documenting this, since it depends on the device. For example, we can see all this further explained for the LED1545G12 light.

Ideally, this would be part of the Light Controller, but there are many features that are not compatible with what Zigbee2MQTT offers:

  • Hold/Click modes (bounce, loop)
  • Color looping
  • Minimum and maximum attribute values

For this reason, there is a separate controller type, Z2M Light Controller, which offers most of the functionality of the Light Controller, but uses the MQTT features from Zigbee2MQTT.

Imagine we have a light with the friendly name livingroom in Zigbee2MQTT and the entity light.livingroom in Home Assistant. Then, let's say we had the following ControllerX configuration for E1810:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller # (1)
  controller: livingroom_controller_action
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: event
  light: light.livingroom
  1. E1810Controller is a Light Controller

This allows us to control the livingroom light with the Light Controller. However, if we replace E1810Controller with E1810Z2MLightController, and light.livingroom with livingroom, we will be using the Z2M Light Controller:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Z2MLightController # (1)
  controller: livingroom_controller_action
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: event
  light: livingroom # (2)
  1. This is a Z2M Light Controller
  2. This is the Zigbee2MQTT friendly name of the light

This sends the MQTT messages through Home Assistant, but if we have the MQTT plugin enabled in AppDaemon, we can send them through the MQTT plugin instead:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Z2MLightController
  controller: livingroom_controller_action
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: event
  light:
    name: livingroom
    mode: mqtt # (1)
  1. mode can either be ha or mqtt (default: ha). On the one hand, ha sends the MQTT messages through Home Assistant with the mqtt.publish service. On the other hand, mqtt sends the MQTT messages through the AppDaemon MQTT plugin (hence skipping HA).

Finally, we can have ControllerX both listening and sending to the MQTT broker directly, without going through Home Assistant:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Z2MLightController
  controller: livingroom_controller # (1)
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
  light:
    name: livingroom
    mode: mqtt
  1. livingroom_controller is the Zigbee2MQTT friendly name of the controller

With this configuration, we can keep using the light even if Home Assistant is down, since all the interactions go:

Zigbee2MQTT <> MQTT Broker <> AppDaemon (ControllerX)

Many of the supported devices have a Zigbee2MQTT light controller class, which can be used in class the same way as their light controller class. Check the supported controllers pages to see the class names.

items.title: Configuration builder
items.text:
Choose your device, what you want to control with it and the integration that receives its events. Then, copy the configuration into your apps.yaml.

The configuration builder needs JavaScript. You can build the configuration by hand following the steps below.

items.title: How the configuration is built
items.text:
Every ControllerX app in apps.yaml links one controller with one entity, and it has the following shape:

livingroom_controller: # (1)!
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller # (2)!
  integration: # (3)!
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
  controller: livingroom_remote # (4)!
  light: light.livingroom # (5)!
  1. A unique name for the app. It can be anything, but each app needs a different one.
  2. The controller class. It depends on the device and on what you want to control (light, media player, switch, cover...). Find it in the page of your device in supported controllers.
  3. The integration that receives the events from the device (Zigbee2MQTT, deCONZ, ZHA, etc.).
  4. The controller ID. Each integration page explains how to find it.
  5. The entity to control. The parameter name depends on the controller type: light, media_player, switch or cover. Read more in type configuration.

The rest of the parameters are optional and are described in configuration and type configuration.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Once ControllerX has been installed, you can proceed to configure ControllerX in apps.yaml: /app_configs/d35634e3_controllerx/apps/apps.yaml with the ControllerX app, or apps.yaml in the AppDaemon apps folder if you installed it manually. This file follows the AppDaemon specifications. Each ControllerX app links one controller with one entity (or group of entities), like:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: <class of your controller>
  controller: <controller id>
  integration: <z2m | deconz | zha | ...>
  light: <light, group entity id>

or:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: <class of your controller>
  controller: <controller entity id>
  integration: <z2m | deconz | zha>
  light:
    name: <light, group entity id>
    color_mode: auto | xy_color | color_temp

or:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: <class of your controller>
  controller: <controller entity id>
  integration: <z2m | deconz | zha>
  media_player: <media player, group entity id>

or:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: <class of your controller>
  controller: <controller entity id>
  integration: <z2m | deconz | zha>
  switch: <switch, group entity id>

Tip

The configuration builder generates this configuration for your device.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
These are the generic app parameters for all types of controllers. The parameters specific to each controller type (light, media player, switch and cover) are described in type configuration.

key type value description module* string controllerx The Python module class* string E1810Controller The Python class. Check the classes for each controller on the supported controllers page. controller* string | list sensor.controller or hue_switch1, hue_switch2 The controller ID, which depends on the integration. Each integration page explains how to find it. integration* string | dict See here the available integrations. The integration through which the device is connected to Home Assistant. actions list All actions This is a list of actions to be included and controlled by the app. To see the actions of each controller, check its page in supported controllers. This attribute cannot be used together with excluded_actions. excluded_actions list Empty list This is a list of actions to be excluded. To see which actions has each controller check the individual controller pages in here. This attribute cannot be used together with actions. action_delta dict | int 300 This is the threshold time between the previous action and the next one (being the same action). If the time difference between the two actions is less than this attribute, then the action won't be called. I recommend changing this if you see the same action being called twice. A different action_delta per action can be defined in a mapping. multiple_click_delay int 500 Indicates the delay (in milliseconds) when a multiple click action should be triggered. The higher the number, the more time there can be between clicks, but there will be more delay for the action to be triggered. action_delay dict | int 0 This can be used to set a delay to each action. By default, the delay for all actions is 0. If defining a map, the key for the map is the action and the value is the delay in seconds. Otherwise, we can set a default time like action_delay: 10, and this will add a delay to all actions. previous_state dict | str - This can be used to restrict when an action is performed depending on the previous state of the entity. This is just applicable for state and z2m (when not listening to MQTT) integrations. For example, it can be used when we want the action to be triggered only with a specific previous state. mapping dict - This can be used to replace the behaviour of the controller and manually select what each button should be doing. By default it will ignore this parameter. Read more about it here. The functionality included in this attribute will remove the default mapping. merge_mapping dict - This can be used to merge the default mapping from the controller and manually select what each button should be doing. By default it will ignore this parameter. Read more about it in here. The functionality included in this attribute is added on top of the default mapping. mode dict | int single This defines what to do when an action is already executing. The options and the behaviour are the same as Home Assistant automation modes since it is based on that. The only difference is that queued only queues 1 task after the one being executed. One can define a mapping for each action event with different modes.

Integration dictionary for integration attribute.

key type value description name* string See here the available integrations. This is the integration that the device was integrated.

In addition, you can add arguments. Each integration has its own arguments.

* Required fields

items.title: Explained with YAML
items.text:
example_app: # It can be anything
  module: controllerx

  # `class` value depends on the controller you want to use
  # Check the classes for each controller on the supported controllers page
  # Supported controller page: https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/controllers/
  class: Controller # or E1810Controller, LightController, HueDimmerController, etc.

  # `controller` value depends on the integration used (z2m, deconz, zha).
  # Each integration page explains how to find it: https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/start/integrations/
  controller: livingroom_controller # or my_controller_id or 00:67:88:56:06:78:9b:3f

  # `integration` is the integration used for your controller
  # It can be a string (e.g. `integration: deconz`) or an object with extra arguments
  # Check https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/start/integrations/ for more info
  integration:
    name: z2m # or deconz, zha, state, mqtt, etc.
    listen_to: mqtt

  # `actions` and `excluded_actions` can be used to indicate which actions from the default mapping
  # will be used or not. These 2 attributes cannot be used at the same time.
  actions: # or excluded_actions. This is optional.
    - toggle
    - brightness_up_click

  # `action_delta` is the threshold to avoid firing the same action twice
  action_delta: 300 # default. This is optional.

  # `multiple_click_delay` is used for the multiclick functionality
  # Check https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/advanced/multiple-clicks for more info
  multiple_click_delay: 500 # default. This is optional.

  # `action_delay` lets you configure delays to existing actions
  action_delay: # This is optional.
    toggle: 10 # This will fire `toggle` action in 10 seconds after pressed.

  # `mode` allows you to define the strategy when an action is already executing
  # Possible values are `single`, `restart`, `queued` and `parallel`
  mode: single # default. This is optional.

  # `mapping` and `merge_mapping` let you override the default behaviour of your controller.
  # `merge_mapping` updates the default mapping, and `mapping` overrides it completely.
  # Check https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/advanced/ for more info
  merge_mapping: # or `mapping`. This is optional.
    brightness_up_click: toggle_full_brightness # use predefined actions
    toggle: # or HA service calls
      service: scene.turn_on
      data:
        entity_id: scene.my_scene
    toggle$2: # These scripts will be called when toggle is fired twice within 500ms (multiple_click_delay)
      - service: script.my_script
      - service: script.my_script_with_arguments
        data:
          my_attr: test

  # From here on, we can include specific attributes from type controllers like
  # Light, MediaPlayer, Switch or Cover controller for example
  # Check https://xaviml.github.io/controllerx/start/type-configuration for more info
  light: light.my_light # or media_player, switch, cover

items.title: Installation
items.text:
ControllerX is an AppDaemon app, so it needs AppDaemon to run. In Home Assistant you can install it in three ways:

Option AppDaemon used How ControllerX is updated Best for ControllerX app (recommended) Its own, built in Update the app from Settings → Apps You only use AppDaemon for ControllerX AppDaemon Store + AppDaemon app The AppDaemon app From the AppDaemon Store UI You already run, or plan to run, other AppDaemon apps Manual The AppDaemon app Download and copy the new release by hand Same as above, without installing AppDaemon Store

Which one should I choose?

  • New to AppDaemon? Use the ControllerX app. It's the simplest setup: one app to install, configure and update.
  • Already using the AppDaemon app for other apps? Install ControllerX in it with AppDaemon Store, so you keep a single AppDaemon instance and get a UI to install and update ControllerX and your other AppDaemon apps.
  • Prefer to manage files yourself? Follow the manual installation.

If you installed ControllerX through HACS, see Migrating from HACS.

Warning

Run only one copy of ControllerX. If the same controller is configured in both the ControllerX app and the AppDaemon app, every button press runs twice (for example, a toggle turns the light on and straight back off).

items.title: ControllerX app (recommended)
items.text:
The ControllerX app runs its own AppDaemon instance with ControllerX preinstalled. Each app update brings the new ControllerX version.

  1. Add the ControllerX app repository to Home Assistant:

    Or go to Settings → Apps → App store, select Repositories in the top-right menu, and add https://github.com/xaviml/controllerx-app.

  2. Install the ControllerX app and start it.

  3. Configure your controllers in /app_configs/d35634e3_controllerx/apps/apps.yaml, for example with the Studio Code Server or Samba share apps. The app creates this file with a commented example on its first start. AppDaemon picks up changes to it without a restart, unless Production mode is on in the app's Configuration tab.

Updating: update the app from Settings → Apps. Your files aren't changed by updates.

Where the app keeps its files 
/app_configs/d35634e3_controllerx/
├── secrets.yaml        Optional, for `!secret` values
└── apps/
    ├── apps.yaml       Your ControllerX configuration
    └── controllerx/    ControllerX code, replaced on every app start

The d35634e3 prefix is the one you get when adding the repository with the button or URL above. If your folder has a different prefix, look for the one ending in _controllerx.

Note

The app's AppDaemon instance is meant only for ControllerX: you can't add other AppDaemon apps to it. If you need other AppDaemon apps, use the AppDaemon Store option instead.

items.title: AppDaemon Store and AppDaemon app
items.text:
AppDaemon Store is a community app that installs and updates AppDaemon apps from GitHub through a UI in the Home Assistant sidebar. It installs them into the AppDaemon app, which runs them. Use this option when you also run other AppDaemon apps, so all of them share a single AppDaemon instance and are managed from one place.

Kudos

Many thanks to mietzen for developing and maintaining AppDaemon Store, which brings back a simple way to install and update AppDaemon apps now that HACS no longer supports them.

  1. Install the AppDaemon app from Settings → Apps → App store and start it once. It creates its folder in /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/.

  2. Add the AppDaemon Store repository to Home Assistant:

    Or go to Settings → Apps → App store, select Repositories in the top-right menu, and add https://github.com/mietzen/hassio-addons.

  3. Install the AppDaemon Store app, start it, and open AppDaemon Store from the sidebar.

  4. Add the xaviml/controllerx repository. ControllerX is installed in /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/apps/controllerx/.
  5. Configure your controllers in /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/apps/apps.yaml.
  6. Restart the AppDaemon app.

Updating: AppDaemon Store checks for new releases and sends a Home Assistant notification when one is available. Update ControllerX from the AppDaemon Store UI, or enable auto-update for it so new releases are installed on their own. Either way, AppDaemon Store restarts the AppDaemon app for you, so the new version is loaded without any manual step.

items.title: Manual installation
items.text:
Use this to install ControllerX in the AppDaemon app without AppDaemon Store, or if you run AppDaemon in some other way (e.g. Docker).

  1. Install the AppDaemon app from Settings → Apps → App store and start it once. It creates its folder in /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/.
  2. Download controllerx.zip from the latest release and unzip it into a controllerx folder in the AppDaemon apps folder, so that you end up with /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/apps/controllerx/controllerx.py. You can copy the files with the Samba share or Studio Code Server apps.
  3. Configure your controllers in /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/apps/apps.yaml.
  4. Restart the AppDaemon app.

Updating: delete the controllerx folder, repeat step 2 with the new release, and restart the AppDaemon app. Your apps.yaml stays as it is. To know when there's a new version, watch the ControllerX releases on GitHub (Watch → Custom → Releases).

items.title: Migrating from HACS
items.text:
HACS no longer supports AppDaemon apps. ControllerX installed through HACS keeps working, but it won't get updates anymore. HACS installed it in /homeassistant/appdaemon/apps/controllerx, next to your apps.yaml. Move to one of the options above:

  • ControllerX app: if you only use AppDaemon for ControllerX, follow Moving to the ControllerX app.
  • AppDaemon Store: if you use other AppDaemon apps, install AppDaemon Store. Its HACS migration assistant detects the HACS setup and, after you confirm, moves your apps and apps.yaml to /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/apps and updates appdaemon.yaml. Then add the xaviml/controllerx repository so AppDaemon Store manages ControllerX from now on.
  • Manual: keep your current folder and update ControllerX by replacing /homeassistant/appdaemon/apps/controllerx with the latest release. Keep the app_dir: /homeassistant/appdaemon/apps line in your appdaemon.yaml; it's what points AppDaemon to this folder.

items.title: Moving to the ControllerX app
items.text:
If ControllerX runs in the AppDaemon app today (installed through HACS, AppDaemon Store or manually), you can move its configuration to the ControllerX app. Your current apps.yaml is in one of these folders:

  • /homeassistant/appdaemon/apps if you installed ControllerX through HACS (some tools show it as /config/appdaemon/apps).

  • /app_configs/a0d7b954_appdaemon/apps otherwise.

  • Install and start the ControllerX app once, so it creates its folder.

  • Copy your apps.yaml to /app_configs/d35634e3_controllerx/apps/apps.yaml. If it also has apps other than ControllerX, remove them from the copy. Don't copy the controllerx folder, the app brings its own.
  • If you use the MQTT plugin, turn on Enable MQTT in the app's Configuration tab. Don't copy the AppDaemon app's appdaemon.yaml: the ControllerX app manages its AppDaemon configuration itself.
  • If your configuration uses !secret, copy those secrets into /app_configs/d35634e3_controllerx/secrets.yaml.
  • Remove ControllerX from the AppDaemon app:
    • If you only used AppDaemon for ControllerX, uninstall the AppDaemon app (and AppDaemon Store, if you had it).
    • Otherwise, remove the ControllerX apps from its apps.yaml, remove ControllerX from AppDaemon Store or delete the controllerx folder, and restart the AppDaemon app.
  • Restart the ControllerX app and check its Log tab.

items.title: Enabling the MQTT plugin (optional)
items.text: If you use the Zigbee2MQTT integration, enable the MQTT plugin, since the Home Assistant sensor listener is deprecated.

items.title: Type Configuration
items.text:
Each device supports one or more controller types, and the controller type defines what the device can control (a light, a media player, a switch or a cover).

Here you can check the specific parameters that each type of controller needs. Check the configuration page for the generic parameters.

items.title: Light controller
items.text:
This controller allows the devices to control a light or a group of lights. It allows you to:

  • Turn on/off light(s)
  • Toggle light(s)
  • Manual increase/decrease of brightness and color
  • Smooth increase/decrease (holding button) of brightness and color
  • Color loop changing if the light supports xy color.
key type value description light* string | dictionary group.livingroom_lights or light.kitchen The light (or group of lights) you want to control manual_steps int 10 Number of steps to go from min to max when clicking. If the value is 2 with one click you will set the light to 50% and with another one to 100%. automatic_steps int 10 Number of steps to go from min to max when holding a button (smooth functionality). min_brightness int 1 The minimum brightness to set to the light. max_brightness int 255 The maximum brightness to set to the light. min_white_value int 1 The minimum white value to set to the light. max_white_value int 255 The maximum white value to set to the light. min_color_temp int 153 The minimum color temperature to set to the light. max_color_temp int 500 The maximum color temperature to set to the light. smooth_power_on boolean False If True the associated light will be set to minimum brightness when brightness up is clicked or held and the light is off. delay int Controller specific Delay in milliseconds between the instructions sent to the light when holding a button (smooth functionality). If it is set to 0, you might get unexpected behavior. max_loops int 50 Maximum number of loops when holding. The loop will stop either with a release action or reaching the max_loops value. hold_release_toggle boolean False If true, a hold action will work as a release when another hold is running. This is useful when you have a button with just one action event and you want to use the hold-release feature, then you just need to map that event to a hold action. release_delay float 0 release actions will be delayed this amount of time (in seconds). This is to avoid cases where release is sent almost at the same time as hold actions. transition int 300 Time in milliseconds the light takes to transition from one state to another. add_transition boolean True If true adds transition if supported, otherwise it does not add the transition attribute. add_transition_turn_toggle boolean True If false does not add transition when turning on/off or toggling, otherwise it adds the transition attribute to the call. See FAQ #6 for a further explanation on the use of this parameter. color_wheel string | list default_color_wheel It defines the color wheel used when changing the xy color with click or hold actions. See the options below. supported_features int 0b101100 or 44 See below for the explanation. supported_color_modes list ["xy", "rgb"] It overrides the supported_color_modes that can be found in light attributes. Values can be color_temp, hs, xy, rgb, rgbw and rgbww. update_supported_features boolean False If true, it will check the supported features field every time before calling any call service action. Useful in case the supported features of the device entity changes over time. hold_toggle_direction_init string up It indicates the first direction of the hold toggle actions (up or down).

* Required fields

Light dictionary for the light attribute:

key type value description name* string light.kitchen The light (or group of lights) you want to control color_mode string auto This attribute can take auto, xy_color or color_temp as value. auto will check first if the light supports xy_color and then color_temp. xy_color will cycle through different colors infinitely. color_temp will change the color temperature attribute of the light. If a light supports both, you can pick which one to use for the light(s).

* Required fields

Information about color_wheel attribute:

This attribute can be either a string or a list. These are the possible string values:

value description default_color_wheel These are the 24 colors that appear in the Home Assistant color wheel. color_temp_wheel These are the xy colors translated from color temperature (2000K to 6488K). They were extracted from here.

Otherwise, a custom xy color list can be defined like the following:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: < device class or LightController >
  controller: < your controller id >
  integration: < your integration >
  light: light.your_light
  color_wheel:
    - [0.525, 0.411]
    - [0.167, 0.338]
    - [0.324, 0.329]

items.title: Zigbee2MQTT Light controller
items.text:
This controller (Z2MLightController) allows the devices to control Zigbee2MQTT lights. It allows you to:

  • Turn on/off light
  • Toggle light
  • Manual increase/decrease of brightness and color
  • Smooth increase/decrease (holding button) of brightness and color

You can read more about this specific controller here.

key type value description light* string | dictionary my_light The light you want to control. This is the Zigbee2MQTT friendly name of the light. click_steps float 70 Number of steps that are passed to Zigbee2MQTT for click actions. hold_steps float 70 Number of steps that are passed to Zigbee2MQTT for hold actions. transition float 0.5 Transition sent to Zigbee2MQTT when changing brightness or color temp. use_onoff bool false This allows click and hold actions to turn on/off the light when off or minimum brightness is reached.

* Required fields

Light dictionary for the light attribute:

key type value description name* string my_light The light you want to control. This is the Zigbee2MQTT friendly name of the light. mode string ha This attribute can take ha or mqtt. On the one hand, ha will send the mqtt messages through Home Assistant with mqtt.publish service. On the other hand, mqtt will send the MQTT messages through MQTT plugin from AppDaemon (hence skipping HA). topic_prefix string zigbee2mqtt MQTT base topic for Zigbee2MQTT MQTT messages. The topic sent will be <topic_prefix>/<friendly_name>/set.

* Required fields

items.title: Media player controller
items.text:
This allows you to control media players. It supports volume, play/pause and skipping forward/backward the track and the source.

key type value description media_player* string group.livingroom_speakers or media_player.bedroom_speaker The media player (or group of media players) you want to control volume_steps int 10 Number of steps to go from min to max when clicking or holding. If the value is 2 with one click you will set the volume to 50% and with another one to 100%. delay int Controller specific Delay in milliseconds between the volume up/down instructions when holding a button. The maximum value is 1000, and if it is set to 0, you might get unexpected behavior. max_loops int 50 Maximum number of loops when holding. The loop will stop either with a release action or reaching the max_loops value. hold_release_toggle boolean False If true, a hold action will work as a release when another hold is running. This is useful when you have a button with just one action event and you want to use the hold-release feature, then you just need to map that event to a hold action. release_delay float 0 release actions will be delayed this amount of time. This is to avoid cases where release is sent almost at the same time as hold actions. supported_features int 0b10111111 or 191 See below for the explanation. update_supported_features boolean False If true, it will check the supported features field every time before calling any call service action. Useful in case the supported features of the device entity changes over time.

* Required fields

items.title: Switch controller
items.text:
This allows you to control switch entities as well as input_boolean and binary_sensor. It supports turning on/off and toggling.

key type value description switch* string group.switches or switch.dishwasher The switch (or group of switches) you want to control

* Required fields

items.title: Cover controller
items.text:
This allows you to control covers. It supports opening, closing and stopping covers.

key type value description cover* string group.all_covers or cover.kitchen The cover (or group of covers) you want to control open_position number 100 The open position (between 0 and 100) close_position number 0 The close position (between 0 and 100) cover_duration number - Duration of the cover to open and/or close in seconds, so toggle_open and toggle_close can stop the cover if the cover is still moving. This is recommended to be used when the cover does not report opening and closing states, otherwise, it is not necessary. supported_features int 0b10111111 or 191 See below for the explanation. update_supported_features boolean False If true, it will check the supported features field every time before calling any call service action. Useful in case the supported features of the device entity changes over time.

* Required fields

items.title: "supported_features" field
items.text: This field will override the supported_features attribute from the entity (light, media player, etc). By default, ControllerX will check this value from Home Assistant, however, sometimes this attribute does not properly reflect the features that the entity supports. ControllerX automatically selects one action or another depending on this value, so it is important that it reflects the supported features. This is defined as a bit field in Home Assistant, so the binary representation of the number defines which features it supports. You can see the values for each entity below.

items.title: Light
items.text:
feature value EFFECT 4 FLASH 8 TRANSITION 32

If you want to express support for everything, the value is 0b101100 or 44.

items.title: Media player
items.text:
feature value PAUSE 1 SEEK 2 VOLUME_SET 4 VOLUME_MUTE 8 PREVIOUS_TRACK 16 NEXT_TRACK 32 TURN_ON 128 TURN_OFF 256 PLAY_MEDIA 512 VOLUME_STEP 1024 SELECT_SOURCE 2048 STOP 4096 CLEAR_PLAYLIST 8192 PLAY 16384 SHUFFLE_SET 32768 SELECT_SOUND_MODE 65536 SUPPORT_BROWSE_MEDIA 131072 SUPPORT_REPEAT_SET 262144 SUPPORT_GROUPING 524288

If you want to express support for everything, the value is 0b1111111111110111111 or 524223.

items.title: Cover
items.text:
feature value OPEN 1 CLOSE 2 SET_COVER_POSITION 4 STOP 8 OPEN_TILT 16 CLOSE_TILT 32 STOP_TILT 64 SET_TILT_POSITION 128

If you want to express support for everything, the value is 0b11111111 or 255.

items.title: Integrations
items.text:
Integrations abstract how ControllerX receives the events from the controllers. Each integration is responsible for listening to a state, an event or an MQTT topic, and for decoding the controller events into actions that ControllerX understands.

These are the integrations supported by ControllerX.

items.title: Integrations with mappings
items.text:
These integrations have a default mapping for specific controllers (see supported controllers).

Integration Configuration value Zigbee2MQTT z2m deCONZ deconz ZHA zha Homematic homematic Lutron Caséta lutron_caseta Shelly shelly Shelly for HASS shellyforhass Tasmota tasmota

items.title: Custom integrations
items.text:
These integrations do not have a default mapping, so they are meant to be used with a custom mapping.

Integration Configuration value State state MQTT mqtt Event event

items.title: Example
items.text:
The integration name can be placed directly in the integration parameter:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  ...
  integration: z2m
  ...

Or in the name parameter inside integration, in case you want to add other integration parameters:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  ...
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
  ...

items.title: deCONZ
items.text: This integration (deconz) listens to deconz_event events, and the action is taken by default from the event attribute of the data object. You can change the attribute that contains the action with the type parameter. In addition, you can select which attribute identifies the controller (id or unique_id) with listen_to.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. deconz listen_to Attribute that identifies the controller (id or unique_id). id type Attribute that contains the action. event

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for deCONZ, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to deconz_event at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the id from the data object of the event.

items.title: Example
items.text:
example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: MFKZQ01LMLightController
  controller: magic_cube
  integration:
    name: deconz
    listen_to: unique_id # defaults to `id`
    type: gesture # defaults to `event`
  light: light.example_light

items.title: Event
items.text: The event integration is meant to be used with any custom Home Assistant event, so it is not tied to a specific integration.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. event event_type* The event we are listening to (e.g. zha_event). - controller_key* The attribute of the controller to listen to (e.g. device_ieee). - action_template* The action template that will be built from the event data (e.g. action_{command}). -

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text:
To find the controller ID for Event, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to the event type you are interested in at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the relevant attribute from the data object of the event.

For further explanation and examples, check here.

items.title: Homematic
items.text: This integration (homematic) listens to homematic.keypress events. It creates an action like <action_type>_<channel>. It does not have any additional arguments.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. homematic

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for Homematic, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to homematic.keypress at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the name from the data object of the event.

items.title: Lutron Caséta
items.text: This integration (lutron_caseta) listens to lutron_caseta_button_event events. It creates an action like button_<number>_<action type>. It does not have any additional arguments.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. lutron_caseta

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for Lutron Caséta, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to lutron_caseta_button_event at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the serial from the data object of the event.

items.title: MQTT
items.text:
This integration (mqtt) listens to the MQTT topic set in the controller attribute. Although this integration is meant to be used with a custom mapping, it also works with the actions from Zigbee2MQTT.

ControllerX listens directly to MQTT rather than to Home Assistant. Not only can you use this with Zigbee2MQTT, but also with any other MQTT integration. This works for JSON and non-JSON payloads. If a specific attribute needs to be extracted from a JSON payload, the key parameter (which works like action_key in the Zigbee2MQTT integration) can be used.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. mqtt key The key to retrieve the data from. -

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: For MQTT, the controller attribute is the MQTT topic to listen to. Unless key is set, the payload of the topic must contain the action name directly, not JSON. This means that when using the MQTT integration with a Zigbee2MQTT controller, the topic to listen to must be zigbee2mqtt/<friendly name>/action or zigbee2mqtt/<friendly name>/click. You can see the topics in the Zigbee2MQTT logs.

items.title: Example
items.text:
example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: LightController
  controller:
    - zigbee2mqtt/stairway_sensor01_occupancy
    - zigbee2mqtt/stairway_sensor02_occupancy
  light: light.stairway
  integration:
    name: mqtt
    key: occupancy
  mapping:
    "true": "on"
    "false": "off"

This example turns on the light when the following payload is published to one of the 2 topics in the controller key:

{
  "battery": 99,
  "illuminance": 0,
  "illuminance_lux": 0,
  "linkquality": 255,
  "occupancy": true,
  "temperature": 27,
  "voltage": 2985
}

Without key, the integration reads non-JSON payloads. Last but not least, the MQTT plugin needs to be enabled.

items.title: Shelly
items.text: This integration (shelly) listens to shelly.click events. It creates an action like <click_type>_<channel>. It does not have any additional arguments.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. shelly

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for Shelly, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to shelly.click at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the device from the data object of the event. You can read more about the event here.

items.title: Shelly for HASS
items.text: This integration (shellyforhass) listens to shellyforhass.click events. It creates an action like <action_type>. It does not have any additional arguments.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. shellyforhass

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for Shelly for HASS, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to shellyforhass.click at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the entity_id from the data object of the event. You can read more about the event here.

items.title: State
items.text: This integration (state) listens to the state changes of an entity, and the new state is used as the action. Add the attribute parameter if you want to listen to the changes of an attribute instead. Read more about the options here.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. state attribute The attribute to listen to for state changes. -

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for State, go to Developer Tools > States and find the entity ID of the sensor you want to use.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Listening for the attribute click from the sensor sensor.my_custom_button:

example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: LightController
  controller: sensor.my_custom_button
  integration:
    name: state
    attribute: click
  light: light.example_light
  mapping:
    1_click: "on"
    2_click: "off"

items.title: Tasmota
items.text: This integration (tasmota) listens to the MQTT topic set in the controller attribute, and gets the action from the attribute defined in component.

items.title: Parameters
How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: The Tasmota integration relies on the MQTT plugin, so the controller is the MQTT topic to listen to (e.g. stat/tasmota_device/RESULT).

items.title: Example
items.text:
example_app:
  module: controllerx
  class: TasmotaButtonLightController
  controller: stat/tasmota_device/RESULT
  integration:
    name: tasmota
    component: Button1
  light: light.example_light

items.title: ZHA
items.text: This integration (zha) listens to zha_event events and builds the action by concatenating the command with its arguments. It does not have any additional arguments.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameter Description Default name* Integration name. zha

* Required fields

items.title: How to extract the controller attribute
items.text: To find the controller ID for ZHA, go to Developer Tools > Events, subscribe to zha_event at the bottom of the page and start listening. Then, press any button on the controller and copy the device_ieee from the data object of the event. It looks like 00:67:88:56:06:78:9b:3f.

items.title: Zigbee2MQTT
items.text: This integration (z2m) is meant to be used with Zigbee2MQTT. It can listen to MQTT topics directly (listen_to: mqtt, recommended), to Home Assistant event entities (listen_to: event) or to the deprecated Home Assistant action sensors (listen_to: ha).

items.title: Parameters
items.text: Parameters Description Default name Integration name z2m listen_to Indicates whether it listens for HA states (ha), MQTT topics (mqtt) or HA Event state (event). ha action_key The key inside the topic payload that contains the fired action from the controller. action action_group A list of allowed action groups for the controller configuration. - topic_prefix MQTT base topic for Zigbee2MQTT MQTT messages. zigbee2mqtt

items.title: MQTT topics listen_to: mqtt
items.text:
Note

This option requires enabling the MQTT plugin.

This is the recommended option. The controller attribute is the friendly name of the controller in Zigbee2MQTT, which can be found in the Zigbee2MQTT configuration of the device.

For example, if the MQTT topic is zigbee2mqtt/livingroom_controller, the friendly name (and controller attribute) of the controller would be livingroom_controller.

items.title: Event state listen_to: event
items.text:
Note

This option requires enabling experimental_event_entities in Zigbee2MQTT. This can be done in Zigbee2MQTT Settings > Home Assistant integration. Then enable Home Assistant experimental event entities. Note that this option is experimental since Zigbee2MQTT 2.0.

To find the controller ID for Zigbee2MQTT, go to Settings > Devices & services > MQTT and select the controller. The parameter you need is the entity ID of the action event without the event. prefix. E.g. if the event is event.livingroom_controller_action, the controller attribute should be livingroom_controller_action.

items.title: HA States (listen_to: ha, deprecated)
items.text:
Warning

This option is deprecated since ControllerX v4.29.0.

Note

This option requires enabling legacy_action_sensor in Zigbee2MQTT. This can be done in Zigbee2MQTT Settings > Home Assistant integration. Then enable Home Assistant legacy action sensors. Note that this option is deprecated since Zigbee2MQTT 2.0 and will be removed in the future.

To find the controller ID for Zigbee2MQTT, go to Settings > Devices & services > MQTT and select the controller. The parameter you need is the entity ID of the sensor that by default finishes in _action.

items.title: Example
items.text:
Imagine we have the following configuration already created for a z2m controller listening to the (deprecated) HA state:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller
  controller: sensor.livingroom_controller_action
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: ha
  light: light.bedroom

Then, if we want to listen to the MQTT topic directly (skipping the HA state machine), we need to change it to:

livingroom_controller:
  module: controllerx
  class: E1810Controller
  controller: livingroom_controller
  integration:
    name: z2m
    listen_to: mqtt
    action_key: action # `action` by default
  light: light.bedroom
